kept.title: Arbitrary Code Execution via untrusted file loading
kept.description: The getHandler function dynamically imports modules based on input filenames provided to the pool.run() task runner. If a user can control the filename or path, they can execute arbitrary code on the worker.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker identifies a service utilizing Tinypool where the 'filename' parameter is user-influenced
Attacker hosts a malicious JavaScript file on the filesystem or accessible path
Attacker triggers a task specifying the malicious file path
Worker process executes the malicious code upon dynamic import
kept.impact: Full compromise of the worker process, leading to data exfiltration or lateral movement.

kept.title: Prototype Pollution via uncontrolled object assignment
kept.description: The serializeError function uses spread syntax to copy all properties from an error object, including potentially malicious prototype properties, which are then transmitted across processes.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker forces an error condition that allows injecting properties into an Error object
Attacker sets properties like '__proto__' or 'constructor' on the error
serializeError spreads these into the new object
The receiving process consumes the object, resulting in prototype pollution
kept.impact: Can lead to cross-process code execution or denial of service via corrupted object states.

kept.title: Use of 'off' rules for critical security linting
kept.description: The ESLint configuration explicitly disables 'no-unsafe-argument', 'no-unsafe-assignment', and 'no-explicit-any' rules, which increases the likelihood of injection and memory-safety vulnerabilities.
steps_to_exploit: Developer introduces unsafe code that would normally be caught by static analysis
The build pipeline passes despite the insecure code patterns
An attacker identifies an entry point for an 'any' typed object to trigger unintended behavior
kept.impact: Security regressions are missed during development, leading to exploitable vulnerabilities in production.

kept.title: Sensitive information leakage in worker messages
kept.description: Unexpected messages on the worker port are serialized and logged via JSON.stringify including the entire message body.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker triggers a malformed message that contains sensitive context data
The worker process receives the message and triggers an error path
The message content is logged to the worker's stdout/stderr, potentially including private task data
kept.impact: Exposure of sensitive operational or user data through system logs.

kept.title: Insecure use of Function constructor for ESM loading
kept.description: The getImportESM function uses the 'new Function' constructor to create a module importer, which is a variation of eval() and can be exploited if input handling is improper.
steps_to_exploit: An attacker finds a way to manipulate the string passed to the constructor
The application executes the injected string as code in the context of the worker
kept.impact: Arbitrary code execution on the worker process.

kept.title: Lack of rate limiting on worker spawning
kept.description: The pool does not implement strict rate limiting on spawn requests during high load, potentially allowing exhaustion of system process/thread limits.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker floods the application with task requests
The pool continuously attempts to spin up new workers if maxThreads isn't reached
System resources (PID, memory) are exhausted
kept.impact: Denial of Service (DoS) of the host operating system.

kept.title: Unsafe serialization of complex objects
kept.description: The system assumes data transmitted between the main process and workers is serializable and safe, but does not sanitize or validate deep object structures before passing them to postMessage.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker crafts a complex object with circular references or getters
The object is sent through a message port
The worker process hangs or crashes during the cloning/deserialization process
kept.impact: Denial of service via resource exhaustion or process crashes.

kept.title: Information disclosure through stack traces
kept.description: The serializeError function includes full stack traces when transmitting errors from workers to the main process.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker triggers an error that exposes sensitive internal file paths
The worker returns the full stack trace to the main process
The main process potentially exposes this stack trace to the end user
kept.impact: Leakage of source code structure and server-side environment details.

kept.title: Race conditions in message handler logic
kept.description: The use of Atomics to manage message counts and a separate port listener can lead to race conditions if the port status changes between checks.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker crafts a high-frequency sequence of tasks
The check for actualResponseCount fails to synchronize perfectly with the port message events
Tasks are processed in an unintended order or dropped
kept.impact: Data inconsistency or potential logical bypasses in task execution.

kept.title: Over-privileged child process spawning
kept.description: Workers are spawned with the full environment of the parent process, which may contain sensitive credentials or tokens.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker compromises the worker process
Attacker reads 'process.env' to capture secrets like AWS keys or database credentials injected into the parent
Attacker exfiltrates credentials

kept.title: Use of unsafe shell-like fork options
kept.description: The process-worker uses 'fork' with options that inherit file descriptors from the parent, potentially leaking sensitive open handles to workers.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker compromises the worker process
Attacker iterates through inherited file descriptors
Attacker accesses sensitive data streams meant only for the parent
kept.impact: Access to restricted resources or sensitive streams.

kept.title: Insecure dependency management policy
kept.description: Dependabot is configured to run daily but without automated security fixes, leaving the project vulnerable to known dependency CVEs.
steps_to_exploit: CVE is published for a dependency like 'vitest' or 'eslint'
Maintainers do not manually update in time
Attacker exploits the known vulnerability to compromise the build/CI system
kept.impact: Increased risk of supply-chain attacks via vulnerable dependencies.

kept.title: Insecure automated release workflow
kept.description: The 'Publish Any Commit' workflow automatically publishes commits to npm. This is extremely dangerous as any contributor or compromised branch could trigger a malicious release.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker submits a Pull Request with a malicious commit
The GitHub Actions workflow automatically builds and publishes the malicious code to the public registry
Users of the package receive the malicious update

kept.title: Improper error handling leads to Zalgo-like behavior
kept.description: The use of throwInNextTick can create unpredictable application states, where errors are thrown outside the original call stack, potentially bypassing global error handlers.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker triggers an edge-case error in the worker setup
The error is caught and passed to throwInNextTick
The application state becomes inconsistent because the error is thrown asynchronously
kept.impact: Instability and potential bypass of security-critical error-handling logic.

kept.title: Unrestricted file path resolution
kept.description: The pool relies on `maybeFileURLToPath` which performs minimal validation on file paths before loading them into a worker.
steps_to_exploit: Attacker passes a path containing '..' or other directory traversal sequences
The pool resolves the path to an unintended directory outside the project root
The worker loads a file from a sensitive system location if the user has read access
kept.impact: Unauthorized file reading or execution via directory traversal.
